title: AI-Driven Shortages in Basic PCB Components Could Be Worse Than 2021 Chip Crisis
content:
AI-Driven Shortages in Basic PCB Components Could Be Worse Than the 2021 Chip Crisis, Report Warns
The AI bubble's insatiable hunger for hardware is impacting supplies of materials for printed circuit boards, says a GEA report.
The electronics industry may be about to experience yet another shortage induced by the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble, but this time in something more fundamental than high-capacity memory components: printed circuit boards (PCBs.)
"Demand for printed circuit boards (PCBs) is outrunning supply at every stage of the chain, from glass fabric and resin to finished boards," a report titled The PCB Squeeze, prepared by the Global Electronics Association, warns. "Fabrication capacity is growing, particularly in Asia, but the limits that matter are upstream: glass, resin, foil, and equipment. Automotive, industrial, medical and defense programs are being crowded out as AI absorbs scarce capacity. Availability, not price, is now the binding risk."
While critics and proponents alike can argue as to the positive and negative impacts of the artificial intelligence bubble, and the large language model (LLM) technology on which it is built, nobody can deny the effect it has had on the electronics industry. Insatiable demand for memory and compute components have seen prices skyrocket, which has directly impacted makers' wallets: popular personal computers, smartphones, and single-board computers are now launching with less RAM and storage or at much higher prices, with some models of Raspberry Pi having more than doubled in price since the bubble's inflation began.
Similar constraints hitting PCB materials and tooling, though, could lead to a much bigger impact — rivaling or even exceeding, the Global Electronics Association projects, the chip shortage crisis of 2021. "Prepreg [pre-impregnated fiberglass pricing] rose about 180% in the year to August 2026," the report explains," and E-glass fabric is up about 140% from its Q3 2025 low. Laminate makers have raised prices repeatedly over the past 12 to 15 months, according to Associate estimates, including increases of up to 30% on laminate and prepreg effective September 1. Shortages — which began in high-end materials for AI servers — have now reached standard grade materials used in automotive, industrial equipment, medical devices, and defense systems."
Unmet demand at the top, then, trickles down — and, if the Association's projections prove accurate, will began to impact anything that uses a printed circuit board, which these days is pretty much anything that uses electricity. Single-board computers will be affected, pushing already-high prices still higher, but so will more affordable devices like microcontroller development boards as-yet largely unaffected by the AI bubble's impact.
"The Association assesses that PCB [supply constraint] exposure may rival the [2021] chip shortage and, in some ways, exceed it, because the shortage reaches the board, the base layer of every electronic system, and the upstream materials are more concentrated and less visible to policymakers," the report warns. "The damage is already spreading. The Association assesses that standard materials will stay constrained through at least the first half of 2027, and that meaningful relief is unlikely before mid-2028."
The takeaway, then: expect more price-hikes to come as we wait for the AI fever to break.
The full report is available to download after free email registration on the Global Electronics Association website.

report.summary: A Global Electronics Association report warns that AI-driven demand is squeezing PCB materials like glass fabric, resin and laminate, potentially causing a shortage worse than 2021's chip crisis.
report.background: The AI boom's demand for compute has already reshaped electronics supply chains: memory and GPU prices have surged, and devices from smartphones to single-board computers ship with less RAM or cost far more—some Raspberry Pi models have more than doubled in price. Until now, most attention focused on chips. But PCBs are the physical substrate every electronic system depends on, and their supply chain is deeper and less visible: glass yarn, E-glass fabric, resin, copper foil, laminate, drilling and imaging equipment. Capacity expansions in Asian fabrication plants take years, while upstream material production is concentrated among few suppliers. Because AI server boards use high-layer-count, high-performance materials, foundries and laminate makers have shifted capacity toward premium grades, leaving standard-grade material—used in cars, industrial controllers, medical devices and defense systems—short. That crowding-out dynamic is what the Global Electronics Association's "The PCB Squeeze" report documents.
key_points: Shortages have moved downstream from AI servers into standard-grade materials. Prepreg pricing rose about 180% in the year to August 2026, E-glass fabric is up roughly 140% from its Q3 2025 low, and laminate makers have pushed through repeated increases—including up to 30% on laminate and prepreg from September 1.

The bottleneck is upstream, not in board fabrication. Fab capacity is expanding, especially in Asia, but glass, resin, foil and equipment are the real limits—so building more factories does not quickly fix the problem, and availability rather than price is now the binding risk.

Non-AI sectors are being crowded out. Automotive, industrial, medical and defense programs are losing allocation priority as AI hardware absorbs scarce material, meaning the shortage spreads well beyond consumer gadgets into long-lifecycle, safety-critical equipment.

Timelines are long. The Association expects standard materials to stay constrained through at least the first half of 2027, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028—a window that could rival or exceed the 2021 chip crisis in duration.

Even cheap hardware is exposed. Unlike the memory crunch, which mostly hit high-end devices, PCB scarcity touches anything with a circuit board—including low-cost microcontroller dev boards that had so far escaped the AI bubble's price effects.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a reminder that compute scaling depends on unglamorous materials, not just GPUs and HBM. Server builders may secure allocation, but they will pay more and face longer lead times, and the political visibility of glass fabric is far lower than that of chips—making subsidies and policy intervention less likely. For developers, the practical effect is hardware prototyping getting slower and pricier: dev boards, SBCs and small production runs will see quotes valid for shorter periods and longer turnaround, so design cycles need buffer stock and earlier ordering. For regular users, expect higher prices and quieter spec cuts across routers, appliances, cars and medical devices—inflationary pressure baked into almost every electronic product, persisting into 2028.
report.tools: To follow and adapt: download "The PCB Squeeze" from the Global Electronics Association site (free email registration). Use open-source KiCad or LibrePCB for designs you can re-spin quickly when parts change, and Octopart or similar BOM tools to track laminate and component availability. OpenPnP suits low-volume in-house assembly when outsourced turns get slow. Watch JLCPCB and PCBWay pricing tiers and lead-time pages as practical shortage barometers, and check Raspberry Pi and other SBC maker price announcements for downstream signals.
